query: What sample sizes and mechanical-replicate counts are needed to detect expected effect sizes in stiffness, energy storage, and fatigue between bow variants?

response.query: What sample sizes and mechanical-replicate counts are needed to detect expected effect sizes in stiffness, energy storage, and fatigue between bow variants?
response.answer: To detect expected effect sizes in stiffness, energy storage, and fatigue between bow variants, sample sizes should be large enough to ensure statistical power, typically 30-50 per group, and mechanical replicates should be at least 5-10 per sample.

results.title: Hydrogen Embrittlement as a Conspicuous Material ...
results.content: HE is the key threat to the structural integrity of metallic materials in green H applications.5−7 Being the smallest atom in the universe, H can adsorb on the surface, diffuse into the bulk, and distribute heterogeneously in and interact with the microstructure of a metal, which can severely undermine the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.8 HE affects nearly all engineering alloys employed in green H transport and storage systems, e.g., ferritic steels,9,10 austenitic stainless steels,11,12 nickel alloys,13−15 aluminum alloys,16 and titanium alloys.17−19 The impact of H extends beyond fracture characteristics to include elasticity, strain hardening, and fatigue life.
